headline: 1.1 is here, and the pillar-saints are in it.
body: Glory to Jesus Christ. Purify 1.1 is here, and the stylites are in it: Symeon the Stylite, Daniel, Symeon of the Wonderful Mountain and Alypius. Four men who spent their lives on top of a column in full view of the world, teaching and settling quarrels from it. They are gathered under a new Stylites heading on the saints index, and their days in the calendar now open to them. Where the old accounts disagree about a year, the profile says so rather than quietly choosing one.
The Hours page now tells you which Hour you are in, and the days with no saint to read about carry a saying of the Desert Fathers instead of an empty page.
Light mode is free for everyone. It is called Light, it sits with the reading settings, and it is yours whether or not you pay for anything, because being able to read is not a premium feature.

Search now opens on a phone and reaches the whole library, the prayers, the saints, the councils and the Scripture. The days with no saint to read about carry a saying of the Desert Fathers instead of an empty page. And the prayer page tells you which Hour you are in.

Two things are right now that were not. Every Lenten Sunday had been showing the previous week's readings, the whole way from Zacchaeus to Palm Sunday. And on the phones the calendar was stuck on the day the app was built, so nothing you tapped moved it. It keeps the real day now, wherever you open it.

Sign in on iPhone works. The app had been throwing your session away on every reload and sending you to the wrong page afterwards, so it looked like signing in had simply failed. That one had kept the app out of the App Store.

What is still not done: prayer reminders cannot be sent yet, most of the saint icons are recorded as unverified rather than guessed at, and the shop's support address needs one database change applied by hand. Those are named in the release notes too. We would rather tell you than let you find out.

headline: Welcome, and glory to Jesus Christ. Here is where the work stands.
body: If you are new here, welcome, and if you have been with us a while, thank you for staying. This note is new: from now on there will be one every week, whether or not a release went out. The version notes below will keep doing what they have always done and tell you exactly what changed. This part is for telling you what we are actually doing and why, which is harder to read off a list of fixes.

This has been a large week for the library. The theology section grew by six long studies, and one of them opens a shelf the app did not have before: the worship of the Church. If you have ever stood through the Divine Liturgy and not known what was happening behind the icon screen, or why the priest goes in and out, or what was being done at the side table before you arrived, there is now a study that walks the service in the order it is actually served. Beside it is a study of the vestments, every garment with its name, its root in the book of Exodus, and the prayer the priest says while putting it on. Nothing about that is decorative. The clergy do not dress for the Liturgy, they are vested, and the prayers say so out loud.

Four more studies come from the harder end of things: why the Orthodox Church does not receive the Council of Florence, and what makes a synod into a Council in the first place. What St Theodore the Studite was really asking of Rome when he wrote to it from exile, read next to the letters he sent to Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem in the same week. Whether St Justin Martyr, writing a century and a half before Nicaea in words the Church had not yet fixed, can fairly be called a subordinationist. And penal substitution: whether Christ died to satisfy a judge or to heal a disease, and why the Fathers refuse to choose.

The part of this week we are most glad about is the part you cannot see. Every one of the seventy five quotations in those six studies was matched word by word against the public domain edition it cites. Two did not survive and were taken out. One of them was a text many of you would recognise on sight, which turned out to be a modern wording wearing a very old citation. We would rather print less and have it be true. That check now runs from a script that lives in the source, so it happens every time rather than the one time somebody thought to look.

Elsewhere: Discover finally lists the saints, which is embarrassing to type, because the words for that row were written months ago and were never connected to anything. Five screens that were built out of line drawings on grey now open on a real image, each one public domain and each one recorded with its source: the Codex Sinaiticus over Scripture, the Deesis over Prayers, the Menologion of Basil II over Discover, the Evangelist Luke at his desk over Reading, and the Ladder of Divine Ascent over your own page.

And some plain repairs. The Prayers tab was carrying a mark meant to be the ancient posture of prayer, arms raised. Drawn without a head or hands and shrunk to the size of a tab, it was two uprights and a crossbar, and more than one of you said so. It is the Orthodox three bar cross now. Scrolling past the end of a page no longer drags the whole screen away from the edge. Searching two references at once inside the Android app no longer throws you back to Today with your query gone. And the last lines of a patristic commentary, which had been hiding underneath the tab bar, are readable again.

What is still ahead: reminders to pray that arrive at your own hour rather than ours, a clearer account section, and a subscription page that tells you plainly what you have and when it renews rather than making you guess. If something here is broken or missing, the Discord is the fastest way to reach us and it is where the editorial work actually happens. Several of the fixes above exist because somebody there took the time to describe exactly what they saw.
